text:
The third example is the complete construction of source Example~4.6.11
\cite[ex.~4.6.11, p.~248]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
Durrett opens that example with its positive half, which holds for every
sub-sigma-algebra \(\mathcal G\) of \(\mathcal F\): if \((X_n)\) is
uniformly integrable and \(X_n\to X\) almost surely, then
\[
          E(X_n\mid\mathcal G)\longrightarrow E(X\mid\mathcal G)
                                      \quad\text{in }L^1.
\]
His route combines Theorem~4.6.3 (here \cref{thm:p15-vitali-convergence}),
which gives \(E|X_n-X|\to 0\), with Exercise~4.6.7 (here item~(1) of
\cref{thm:p15-changing-conditional-limits}, taken with
\(\mathcal F_n=\mathcal G\) for every \(n\)). The third example shows
that this conclusion in mean cannot be strengthened to almost-sure
convergence, even though the sequence itself converges almost surely and
in \(L^1\).

For the positive half stated before the third example, let
\(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a sub-sigma-algebra, let
\((X_n)\) be uniformly integrable, and let \(X_n\to X\) almost surely,
with \(X\) real and measurable. Almost-sure convergence gives
convergence in probability. Fix \(\epsilon>0\). The countable suprema
\(\sup_{m\geq n}|X_m-X|\) are measurable, the events
\(\{\sup_{m\geq n}|X_m-X|>\epsilon\}\) decrease in \(n\), and their
intersection lies in the null event on which \(X_m\) does not converge
to \(X\). Continuity from above gives
\[
 P(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)\leq
       P\Bigl(\sup_{m\geq n}|X_m-X|>\epsilon\Bigr)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The implication from the first to the second condition of
\cref{thm:p15-vitali-convergence} now gives \(X\in L^1\) and
\(E|X_n-X|\to 0\). Put \(\mathcal F_n=\mathcal G\) for every \(n\).
This sequence increases and
\(\mathcal F_\infty=\sigma(\mathcal G)=\mathcal G\), so item~(1) of
\cref{thm:p15-changing-conditional-limits} gives
\(E(X_n\mid\mathcal G)\to E(X\mid\mathcal G)\) in \(L^1\).
In the third example \(X=0\) and \(E(X_n\mid\mathcal G)=B_n\), and this
conclusion is the limit \(E|B_n|\to 0\) computed above.

Durrett states the hypothesis with a real level \(x\) in place of
\(K\): a bound \(\delta(x)>0\) for \(P(D\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n)\), almost
surely on \(\{X_n\leq x\}\) \cite[ex.~4.6.4]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
The two forms are equivalent because the events \(\{X_n\leq x\}\)
increase with \(x\); the annex proof records the reduction.

text:
The real-level form of the hypothesis is equivalent to the integer form
used here. Given bounds \(\delta(x)\) for every real level \(x\geq0\),
put \(\delta_K=\delta(K)\). Conversely, given the integer bounds and a
real level \(x\geq0\), choose a positive integer \(K\geq x\); then
\(\{X_n\leq x\}\subseteq\{X_n\leq K\}\), so \(\delta(x)=\delta_K\)
bounds \(P(D\mid\mathcal F_n)\) from below almost surely on
\(\{X_n\leq x\}\). The conclusion therefore holds under either form.
reason: Annex counterpart of the preceding entry: the reduction between Durrett's real-level hypothesis (Ex. 4.6.4, printed p. 249) and the host's integer thresholds, with its proof.
